topicPacks.title: Eye Anatomy

cards.definition:
Organ that focuses light onto the retina for visual processing.
Orientation: Front = cornea; back = retina and optic nerve; vitreous fills most of the interior.

Transparent front surface supplying most of the eye's refractive power.
Location: Transparent dome at the very front, in front of the aqueous-filled anterior chamber.

Tough outer coat that supports and protects the eye.
Location: Outer white coat; joins the cornea at the limbus.

Thin membrane covering the visible sclera and inner eyelids.
Location: Covers the visible sclera, not the corneal surface.

Pigmented muscular structure controlling pupil size.
Location: Behind the cornea and aqueous; in front of the crystalline lens.

Adjustable opening in the iris through which light enters.
Location: Central hole of the iris, in front of the lens; not a physical tissue.

Flexible transparent structure that fine-tunes focus.
Location: Behind the iris/pupil and in front of the vitreous; held by zonules.

Changes lens shape during accommodation.
Location: Ring in the ciliary body around the lens; relaxation/tension changes zonular pull.

Fibers suspending the lens and transmitting ciliary forces.
Location: Run from ciliary body to lens capsule.

Fluid-filled space between cornea and iris.
Location: Between posterior corneal surface and anterior iris surface; contains aqueous, not vitreous.

Clear fluid nourishing anterior eye tissues and maintaining pressure.
Location: Circulates through posterior and anterior chambers; distinct from vitreous gel.

Large space behind the lens and in front of the retina.
Location: Posterior to the lens, bounded by retina and other posterior ocular tissues.

Transparent gel-like material filling the vitreous chamber.
Location: Fills the vitreous chamber; its collagen/hyaluronan organization matters for floaters.

Light-sensitive neural tissue converting photoreceptor responses into signals processed by retinal circuits.
Location: Innermost neural layer lining the back of the eye, adjacent to the vitreous.

Central retinal region specialized for detailed vision.
Location: Central posterior retina; surrounds the fovea.

Central macular pit with very high cone density and sharp vision.
Location: Center of the macula; densely packed cones support high acuity.

Exit region of optic nerve fibers; lacks photoreceptors.
Location: On the nasal side of the retinal posterior pole; normal physiological blind spot.

Axons of retinal ganglion cells carrying visual information toward the brain.
Connection: Ganglion-cell axons exit at the optic disc and project toward visual centers.

Vascular tissue nourishing the outer retina.
Location: Between sclera and retina/RPE; highly vascular.

Cell layer supporting photoreceptors and absorbing stray light.
Location: Monolayer between photoreceptors and choroid.

topicPacks.studyNote: Learn the order light traverses: cornea → aqueous/pupil → lens → vitreous → retina. Also locate layers and chambers.

cards.definition:
Bending of light when it passes between media with different refractive indices.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Adjustment of lens power to focus at different distances.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Optical state in which distant objects focus on the retina without accommodation.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Distant light focuses in front of the retina when accommodation is relaxed.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Distant light tends to focus behind the retina without accommodation.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Different optical powers across meridians cause uneven focus.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Retinal rod or cone cell that converts absorbed light into a change in electrical signaling.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Photoreceptors specialized for sensitivity at low light levels.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Photoreceptors supporting color and high-acuity daylight vision.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Conversion of absorbed photons into electrical changes in photoreceptors.
Mechanism: Light hyperpolarizes rods and cones and alters neurotransmitter release.

Relay photoreceptor signals toward ganglion cells.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Retinal neurons whose axons form the optic nerve.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Retina → optic nerve → thalamic LGN → visual cortex, with additional pathways.
Detail: Most conscious vision routes via the lateral geniculate nucleus to occipital cortex.

Ability to resolve fine spatial details.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Ability to detect brightness differences across spatial scales.
Floater link: Contrast may worsen even if standard high-contrast visual acuity remains good.

Change in visual sensitivity with prevailing lighting.
Research link: Separate optical image quality from retinal coding and conscious vision.

Visual experience caused by structures or processes within the eye.
Example: Vitreous floater shadows are perceived because of structures within the observer’s eye.

Spatial distribution of incoming light formed on the retina.
Simulation link: A retinal irradiance map is a physical prediction, not the final conscious percept.

Subjective experience constructed by visual processing, not a retinal photograph.
Research link: A participant-matched image measures reported perception, not actual floater anatomy.

topicPacks.studyNote: The eye creates a retinal signal, but the brain determines perception; visual acuity ≠ contrast sensitivity.

topicPacks.title: Vitreous Biology

cards.definition:
Mostly water, with a collagen network, hyaluronan, and other constituents.
Context: Its high water content does not mean it behaves like simple water; its matrix affects motion.

Fine structural fibers contributing to the vitreous framework.
Floater link: Aggregated or reorganized fibers may create refractive-index disturbances.

Water-binding polymer helping maintain vitreous gel properties.
Role: Helps maintain hydration and separation of collagen fibrils in the vitreous matrix.

Outer region of the vitreous adjacent to ocular structures.
Location: Thin peripheral condensed vitreous, including its posterior retinal-facing portion.

Boundary where vitreous cortex interacts with the retinal surface.
Research link: Traction here is relevant to PVD, tears and some visual symptoms.

Region of especially firm vitreous attachment near the retinal periphery.
Location: Straddles the ora serrata region; unusually strong attachment.

Formation or enlargement of liquid regions within the vitreous gel.
Distinction: Liquefaction can occur without complete posterior vitreous detachment.

Structural aggregation and contraction of vitreous gel, often accompanying liquefaction.
Distinction: Structural collapse and liquefaction are related but not identical changes.

Separation of posterior vitreous cortex from the retina.
Important: Common with aging but floaters can exist without PVD; acute symptoms merit examination.

Ring-shaped opacity sometimes seen after vitreous separation near the optic disc.
Location: May arise from tissue around the optic nerve head after PVD; not present in every PVD.

Structure or material in vitreous that alters light transmission.
Important: A transparent refractive-index difference may still alter retinal illumination.

Perception of mobile spots, threads, or other vitreous-related shadows.
Clinical distinction: Symptom name; it does not identify a unique anatomical cause.

Vitreous opacities associated with bothersome visual symptoms.
Research link: Reported bother, functional contrast and imaging findings need not agree.

Floaters present without a posterior vitreous detachment.
Important: No-PVD status should be confirmed clinically, not inferred from age alone.

Structural changes in the gel that may create opacities and liquid spaces.
Risk context: Myopia, aging and ocular inflammation can influence vitreous changes.

Physical size, shape, orientation, and distribution of an opacity.
Simulation link: Represent strands, sheets or aggregates instead of assuming only dark circles.

How an opacity moves in the vitreous with eye motion and internal fluid forces.
Simulation link: Inertia, vitreous mechanics and eye motion affect perceived trajectories.

Three-dimensional position of an opacity relative to the lens and retina.
Simulation link: Use 3D depth, not only x/y, because retinal pattern depends on distance.

New flashes, sudden floater increase or curtain-like visual loss can indicate retinal pathology.
Safety: Sudden flashes, many new floaters, or a field curtain warrant urgent dilated retinal assessment.

topicPacks.studyNote: Understand why a mostly transparent collagen/hyaluronan gel can contain symptomatic optical structures.

topicPacks.title: Fundamental Optics

cards.definition:
Geometric approximation showing the direction of light propagation.
Research link: Relate this physical quantity to predicted retinal illumination patterns.

Surface joining points of equal optical phase.
Simulation link: Numerical wavefront phase makes diffraction and interference computable.

Distance between repeating phases of a wave; affects diffraction and color.
Unit: Usually nanometers for visible light; polychromatic white light needs wavelength integration.

Ratio of light speed in vacuum to its phase speed in a medium.
Floater link: Small contrast between opacity and vitreous may still create optical effects.

n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂; relates incident and refracted angles.
Application: Ray tracing through cornea and lens interfaces.

Light returning from a boundary between media.
Floater link: Backscattered/reflected signal may be weak even when subjective effect is strong.

Redistribution of light into other propagation directions.
Floater link: Light is redistributed, so a simple black blocking mask may be misleading.

Conversion of light energy into other forms within matter.
Distinction: Loss of transmitted energy is different from phase alteration by a clear structure.

Fraction of incident light passing through a system.
Caution: For coherent waves, use complex amplitude transmission, not intensity alone.

Logarithmic measure of attenuation; often OD = −log₁₀(T).
Caution: OD summarizes attenuation, not all phase-induced interference effects.

Wave spreading/interference around edges or through apertures.
Floater link: Edges and fine structures can produce nontrivial retinal intensity patterns.

Combination of waves according to their phase relationships.
Floater link: Light waves can reinforce or cancel, changing retinal brightness.

Image intensity pattern produced by an ideal point source.
Limitation: A single global PSF need not describe position-dependent opacity effects.

Operation combining an image with a spatial response or blur kernel.
Condition: Simple convolution assumes a linear, approximately shift-invariant imaging system.

Opening restricting which rays or waves pass through an optical system.
Eye link: The iris pupil is an adjustable aperture, altering illumination angular range.

Range of object distances appearing acceptably sharp.
Distinction: Apparent floater sharpness is not the same as ordinary external-scene focus.

Radiant power arriving per unit area, typically W/m².
Simulation output: Compute relative or calibrated retinal irradiance at each position.

Photometric measure of light from a surface in a direction, in cd/m².
Experiment link: Monitor luminance requires calibrated display conditions for comparisons.

(Imax − Imin)/(Imax + Imin), useful for repeating patterns.
Use: Appropriate for bright/dark periodic gratings; also specify contrast conventions.

(I − Ibackground)/Ibackground, useful for small targets on uniform backgrounds.
Use: Small targets on a near-uniform background; contrast may be negative for dark targets.

Number of light-dark cycles per degree of visual angle or other distance unit.
Unit: Cycles/degree for perception; cycles/mm for physical image-plane measures.

How strongly an optical system preserves contrast at each spatial frequency.
Connection: Optical contrast transfer is distinct from overall human contrast sensitivity.

topicPacks.studyNote: Ask whether a prediction requires rays, wave phase, physical radiometry or perceptual contrast.

topicPacks.title: Optics of Floater Perception

cards.definition:
Retinal illumination disturbance associated with a vitreous opacity.
Precision: A pattern of retinal irradiance variation; often includes phase/diffraction effects.

cards.term: Why visible on bright uniform backgrounds?
cards.definition:
Uniform scenes can make localized contrast disturbances easier to notice.
Nuance: Background statistics and adaptation matter; more photons alone do not explain visibility.

It changes the range of incident light paths and resulting shadow structure.
Literature: A 2022 Fourier-optics model predicted stronger effects for constricted pupils.

Opacity-retina separation affects shadow spread and structure.
Model link: Change axial position and compare pattern width, edges and local contrast.

cards.term: Does a floater simply block light?
cards.definition:
Not always; refraction, scattering, diffraction, and absorption may all contribute.
Literature: Even weakly contrasting transparent structures can be symptomatic.

Perceived image depends on optical propagation and visual processing.
Inference: Reconstructing perception cannot uniquely recover original 3D anatomy.

Degree of spatial edge definition in the retinal intensity pattern.
Measure: Can be operationalized via edge-spread width or local spatial gradients.

Partially illuminated region around a shadow due to light-source or aperture geometry.
Model link: Varies with source angular extent, pupil geometry and object separation.

Size expressed as the visual angle subtended at the eye.
Experiment: Use visual angle when comparing patterns across monitors/viewing distances.

Opacities can move relative to the retina and continue drifting after a saccade.
Research design: Record gaze or standardize eye movements for motion experiments.

Rapid eye movement shifting the point of gaze.
Floater link: Internal structures may lag eye motion, creating after-movement drift.

Maintaining gaze on a target to control retinal positioning.
Experiment: A fixation marker reduces uncontrolled changes in retinal coordinates.

Difference between the opacity's and vitreous's refractive indices.
Wave model: Difference in optical path length can alter phase without strong absorption.

Computed 2D field of light intensity across retinal positions.
Output: Compare baseline versus opacity-present patterns with quantitative contrast metrics.

Optical amplitude/phase distribution at the pupil used in wave-optics models.
Software link: Model as complex array with amplitude and phase.

A dark sprite can mimic appearance but does not establish physical accuracy.
Use: Good for matching subjective reports; inadequate to claim physical optical validation.

topicPacks.studyNote: A floater is an optical perturbation, not merely a dark sprite. Depth and pupil are key candidate parameters.

Floater example: Input pupil + opacity geometry + wavelength → retinal intensity distribution.

Uses observed outputs to estimate model parameters, often non-uniquely.
Floater caution: Multiple opacity depths/shapes may produce similar perceptual matches.

Adjustable quantity representing a property of the modeled system.
Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Numerically follows light rays through surfaces and media.
Use: Understand geometric paths through cornea, pupil and lens before wave calculations.

Models light using complex fields, propagation, and interference.
Use: Essential when phase, interference and diffraction affect predicted patterns.

Uses Fourier transforms to analyze imaging and diffraction.
Floater reference: Harmer et al. (2022) used it to model vitreous opacity effects.

Approximate wave propagation suitable for many near-field geometries.
Use: Propagate complex fields between nearby optical planes; check approximation assumptions.

Far-field diffraction approximation or equivalent focal-plane regime.
Use: Appropriate in the far field or focal-plane geometry, not for every floater depth.

Amplitude and phase representation of a light wave.
Data model: A 2D array of complex numbers holds amplitude and phase.

Position within a wave cycle; crucial to interference.
Floater link: A transparent opacity may shift phase and cause interference without blocking light.

For a coherent scalar field, intensity is proportional to |U|².
Caution: For broadband or incoherent sources, combine contributions appropriately.

Grid representing opacity outline or spatially varying transmission.
Caution: A binary opaque mask is only a baseline; complex transmission is more general.

Voxel representation of an object's spatial extent and optical properties.
Use: Study depth-dependent distribution rather than only an image-plane sprite.

Three-dimensional counterpart of an image pixel.
Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Converting continuous geometry into a discrete pixel grid.
Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Spatial or temporal sampling density used by a simulation.
Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Interval between successive simulated states.
Research link: Record this in the model specification and test its numerical consequences.

Systematically varying inputs to study their effects on outputs.
Example: Compare shadow contrast across pupil diameter and floater-retina distance.

Assessing how model outputs respond to changes in inputs.
Goal: Identify parameters that most influence visibility, guiding experiments.

Whether distinct parameter values can be distinguished from available observations.
Research limit: A visually matched simulated floater is not automatically a unique diagnosis.

A feature caused by modeling or numerical choices, not underlying physics.
Test: Change numerical grid and verify predicted fringe patterns remain stable.

topicPacks.studyNote: Distinguish a forward optical solver, inverse parameter estimation, and illustrative rendering.

topicPacks.title: Integrative Reasoning

cards.definition:
Represent pupil, optical media, opacity, and retina with model geometry and parameters.
Bridge: Cornea/lens = focusing elements; iris = aperture; vitreous opacity = perturbation.

Translate propagation laws into numerical operations on rays, fields, or arrays.
Thesis goal: Connect a defined biological assumption to a testable computational prediction.

Change one controlled input and quantify a defined output.
Thesis goal: Connect a defined biological assumption to a testable computational prediction.

Neural processing means retinal illumination is not identical to conscious appearance.
Research: Treat optical output and subjective report as separate validation targets.

cards.term: Why start with a simple model?
cards.definition:
It tests assumptions and code before adding complex physics.
Thesis goal: Connect a defined biological assumption to a testable computational prediction.

When diffraction or interference materially affects the intended prediction.
Thesis goal: Connect a defined biological assumption to a testable computational prediction.

Thesis goal: Connect a defined biological assumption to a testable computational prediction.

topicPacks.title: Clinical Conditions and Assessment
topicPacks.studyNote: Differentiate floater symptoms from other eye disease; recognize clinical measurement limits.

cards.definition:
Clouding of the crystalline lens, not the vitreous.
Contrast: Cataracts mainly affect focused light before it enters the vitreous.

Progressive optic neuropathy often associated with characteristic visual-field loss.
Contrast: An optic-nerve disease, not a vitreous opacity.

Disease of the central macula impairing detailed vision.
Location: Retina at the back of the eye, not the vitreous cavity.

Diabetes-related retinal vascular damage.
Clinical link: Bleeding into the vitreous may also cause sudden floaters.

Separation of neurosensory retina from underlying supporting tissues.
Safety: New curtain-like field loss is an emergency assessment indication.

Inflammation of uveal tissues, sometimes with vitreous inflammatory cells.
Differential: Floaters can reflect inflammation, not just collagen aggregates.

Clinical examination of retina and vitreous through a dilated pupil.
Use: Important for ruling out retinal tears in symptomatic cases.

Cross-sectional imaging using low-coherence light interferometry.
Limit: Standard retinal OCT does not fully visualize all vitreous opacities.

Ultrasound imaging of ocular structures through reflected sound.
Use: Can assess vitreous echoes and posterior segment when optical viewing is limited.

Ultrasound-based attempt to measure vitreous echo characteristics.
Research: An objective structural metric that may complement symptom reports.

Sensitivity to contrast across a range of spatial frequencies.
Research: May reveal floater-related functional deficits missed by acuity testing.

Structured questionnaire reporting symptoms or quality of life.
Research: Keep reported functional impact distinct from imaging findings.

Surgery removing vitreous gel, sometimes considered for severe symptoms.
Caution: Invasive and associated with meaningful ocular risks.

Laser treatment intended to disrupt selected vitreous opacities.
Evidence: Benefits and risks vary; do not assume established effectiveness for all floaters.

Change in perceptual response as the nervous system adapts to stimuli.
Caution: Perceived improvement need not mean the opacity disappeared.
